fixes.explanation: That's the word Paul uses, baker. If she is joined to another man while her husband is still alive, she is called an adulteress (Romans 7:3). The timing is the whole point. Same woman, same other man, but everything depends on whether her husband is still living.

Moses, Israel's leader, is the one the law was given through (John 1:17), so I get the pick. But Paul says they died to the law so that they might belong to Him who was raised from the dead (Romans 7:4). That's Christ, not Moses. The new belonging is to a risen person.

Abraham is called the father of us all in Romans 4:16, so he's a fair guess. But in this verse Paul says they died to the law that they might belong to Him who was raised from the dead (Romans 7:4). Paul is pointing to Christ.
Paul writes to all in Rome who are loved by God (Romans 1:7), so I see how that one slid in. But Paul says the fruit is borne to God (Romans 7:4). Rome isn't who the fruit is for. God is.

The world is a fair guess, friend, but it's not in this sentence. Paul says the sinful passions were aroused by the law (Romans 7:5). That's a strange thing to hear, and he stops to explain it soon after.

That's right, baker. Paul says we have been released from the law so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit (Romans 7:6). The service doesn't stop. What changes is the way it's done. I know a bit about getting pulled out of a dark junk drawer and handed a new job, and it's a good feeling.
Paul says the opposite, baker. He asks, "Is the law sin?" and answers, "Certainly not!" (Romans 7:7) He says it plainly. The law is not sin.

That's his example, baker. Paul says he would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, "Do not covet." (Romans 7:7) It's the one sin he names here. The command named it, and then he knew.

Paul does tell believers not to lie to one another (Colossians 3:9), so I get the guess. But it's not the one he picks here. He says he would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, "Do not covet." (Romans 7:7) Coveting is his one example, and that's the word he uses.
